clinicalPearls: Management is driven by clinical phenotype and by left ventricular ejection fraction: HFrEF (LVEF <=40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (>=50%); the older terms systolic and diastolic heart failure have been abandoned because most patients have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.1987, 1978).

The disease is staged along the ACC/AHA framework: stage A (at risk), stage B (asymptomatic structural/ventricular dysfunction), stage C (symptomatic HF), and stage D (advanced/refractory HF); approach to therapy escalates across these stages (Harrison 22e p.1987).

Stage B asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction is treated to facilitate ventricular recovery and prevent progression to clinical HF, whereas stage D carries a high risk of death from sudden death or end-stage pump failure and may prompt consideration of transplant, mechanical circulatory support, or palliative care (Harrison 22e p.1987).

The robust randomized-trial evidence base supporting disease-modifying therapy applies to HFrEF (LVEF <=40%); historically HFmrEF and HFpEF management was symptom-focused owing to lack of outcome-improving therapies (Harrison 22e p.1987).

Even with effective therapy, patients across all EF categories remain at risk for clinical deterioration, typically from progressive sodium and fluid retention that drives congestive symptoms and acute decompensated HF (Harrison 22e p.1987).

Trials of agents that improve outcomes in HFrEF (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, digoxin, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) have generally been unsuccessful when exported to HFpEF, with several large trials showing reduced HF hospitalizations but no all-cause mortality benefit (Harrison 22e p.1987-1988).

Management of HFpEF has centered on lifestyle modification, control of congestion, rhythm stabilization (especially atrial fibrillation), blood pressure control to guideline targets, and treatment of comorbidities such as obesity, obstructive lung disease, sleep apnea, diabetes/insulin resistance, anemia, iron deficiency, and chronic kidney disease (Harrison 22e p.1987).

A favorable signal for spironolactone in HFpEF emerged mainly from the subgroup randomized in the Americas in the TOPCAT trial, supporting only a weak guideline recommendation in selected patients at low risk for hyperkalemia and worsening renal function (Harrison 22e p.1988).

The microvascular endothelial inflammation paradigm proposes that comorbidity-driven inflammation impairs nitric oxide signaling and increases myocardial stiffness in HFpEF; trials enhancing NO bioavailability (sildenafil in RELAX, nitrates in NEAT-HFpEF, inorganic nitrite in INDIE-HFpEF) failed to improve functional capacity or quality of life (Harrison 22e p.1988-1989).

Approximately one-half of patients with HF have reduced EF and one-half have preserved or mildly reduced EF; classifying by EF matters because of differences in demographics, comorbidities, and treatment response (Harrison 22e p.1978).

Acute heart failure (formerly acute decompensated HF) refers to rapid onset or worsening of symptoms; most episodes are decompensations of chronic HF, but roughly 20% are new-onset, occurring with acute coronary syndrome, acute valvular dysfunction, hypertensive urgency, or postcardiotomy syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1976).

HF with recovered EF (HFrecEF) is a subgroup whose EF normalizes on therapy; predictors include younger age, shorter HF duration, nonischemic etiology, smaller ventricular volumes, and absence of fibrosis, and withdrawal of disease-modifying therapy can cause recurrence in up to half of patients within 6 months (Harrison 22e p.1977).
harrison.pathophysiology: HFrEF is a progressive disorder in which an index event (acute myocardial infarction, chronic pressure or volume overload, inherited or congenital disease) is followed by months to years of cardiovascular remodeling. Concentric hypertrophy reduces wall stress in pressure overload, while eccentric hypertrophy (chamber dilation) occurs in volume overload; remodeling involves myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, altered calcium handling, fetal gene reexpression, necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy. Maladaptive activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports cardiac output but ultimately produces excessive vasoconstriction, volume retention, electrolyte and renal abnormalities, baroreceptor dysfunction, direct myocardial toxicity, and arrhythmias, with antagonism of these systems shown to attenuate or reverse remodeling and reduce mortality. Counterregulatory vasodilatory hormones (ANP, BNP, prostaglandins, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, nitric oxide) are upregulated; neprilysin inactivates natriuretic peptides and bradykinin, the rationale for angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition. Endothelin, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6), and reactive oxygen species contribute to remodeling, and the cardiorenal syndrome reflects both reduced forward flow and systemic venous/abdominal congestion. HFpEF pathophysiology is less defined and involves diastolic dysfunction together with vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, comorbidity-driven microvascular inflammation, and impaired nitric oxide/cGMP/protein kinase G signaling causing myocardial stiffening (Harrison 22e p.1978-1982, 1989).

redFlags: Acute pulmonary edema with severe dyspnea and pink frothy sputum due to markedly elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
Hypotension with narrow pulse pressure and a rapid, thready pulse indicating severe low-output state
Pulsus alternans and an audible S3 gallop signaling severe hemodynamic compromise and adverse prognosis
Kussmaul's sign (inspiratory rise in JVP) as a marker of severe biventricular failure and poor outcome
Marked elevation of transaminases and lactic acid suggesting cardiogenic shock with severe low output
Oliguria from severe reduction in renal blood flow indicating advanced-stage HF
Cheyne-Stokes / periodic breathing and central sleep apnea in advanced HF
Cardiac cachexia (edema-free weight loss >5% over 12 months) and frailty/sarcopenia in longstanding severe HF
Recurrent acute decompensated HF despite optimal therapy heralding advanced (stage D) refractory disease
harrison.prognosis: Overall 5-year survival after a primary-care diagnosis of HF is about 50%, and 1-year mortality may reach 40% in severe HF. After an HF admission, mortality ranges from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission rates of 20-25% at 60 days approaching 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Most deaths are cardiovascular, from progressive pump failure or sudden cardiac death. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, coronary disease, advanced NYHA class, presence of an S3 or elevated JVP, reduced LV/RV ejection fraction, elevated wedge pressure, low cardiac index, reduced peak VO2, pulmonary hypertension, worsening renal function, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, elevated troponin and natriuretic peptides, raised neurohormones, tachycardia, wide QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular ectopy. Black patients have higher case-fatality rates and there is regional variation (highest in the US Midwest and rural areas). HFrecEF generally carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF. Overall outcomes are improving with guideline-directed therapy and risk-factor control (Harrison 22e p.1976-1977).
pitfalls: Signs and symptoms of HF are neither sensitive nor specific, so a high index of suspicion is needed, especially in older patients with hypertension, diabetes, or CKD (Harrison 22e p.1985).
Right HF with hepatic congestion can elevate transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin and be misdiagnosed as biliary tract disease (Harrison 22e p.1984).
Cardiac asthma (wheezing and rhonchi from bronchial congestion) can be mistaken for asthma or COPD and treated inappropriately (Harrison 22e p.1983).
Rales may be absent in longstanding HF with chronically elevated wedge pressures because of increased lymphatic drainage, so their absence does not exclude congestion (Harrison 22e p.1983).
NYHA functional class correlates poorly with objective measures of cardiac structure (LV size, EF) and function (peak VO2) (Harrison 22e p.1982).
Natriuretic peptide levels may be falsely low in obesity and elevated by noncardiac factors (age, female sex, CKD) and other cardiac conditions, limiting interpretation (Harrison 22e p.1985).

Lower extremity edema may be absent in acute HF or in younger adults despite marked systemic venous hypertension; unilateral edema suggests DVT, prior trauma, or vein harvest rather than HF (Harrison 22e p.1984).
Drugs causing salt/water retention (NSAIDs) or negative inotropy (calcium channel blockers) can precipitate decompensation and should be recognized as provider-related triggers (Harrison 22e p.1983).
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, RAAS inhibitors, and potassium supplements can cause hyperkalemia, particularly with reduced GFR, requiring monitoring (Harrison 22e p.1984-1985).
harrison.severityClassification: Two complementary frameworks are used. The NYHA functional classification grades symptom-limiting activity: class I (no limitation), class II (mild; symptoms with ordinary activity), class III (moderate; symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity), and class IV (severe; symptoms at rest worsening with any activity). The ACC/AHA staging is progressive and irreversible: stage A (at risk, no structural disease or symptoms), stage B (structural disease/asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction without symptoms), stage C (structural disease with current or prior symptoms), and stage D (advanced/refractory HF requiring specialized interventions). Patients are additionally phenotyped by ejection fraction: HFrEF (LVEF <=40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (>=50%) (Harrison 22e p.1982-1983, 1987).
management: Establish disease-modifying therapy in HFrEF with the four pillars: an angiotensin-receptor-neprilysin inhibitor or ACE inhibitor, a beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor, up-titrated to tolerance
Relieve congestion and fluid retention with loop diuretics titrated to symptoms and volume status
Offer device therapy where indicated, with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for sudden-death prevention and cardiac resynchronisation for prolonged QRS with left bundle branch block
Treat HFmrEF and HFpEF with an SGLT2 inhibitor and diuretics for congestion while managing hypertension and other comorbidities
Address the underlying cause and precipitants such as ischaemia, valvular disease, and atrial fibrillation, and advise sodium and fluid moderation
Escalate advanced, refractory (stage D) disease to transplantation, mechanical circulatory support, or palliative care
Monitor daily weights, symptoms, renal function and electrolytes, and natriuretic peptides through a specialist heart-failure service with patient education
